title: Al-Malik al-Nasir and the Three Chiefs of Police

full_text:
Sultan Al-Malik al-Nasir of Cairo sat upon his throne in the Citadel, holding council with the three chiefs of police who governed the quarters of Cairo, Fustat, and Qus. Desiring to test their wisdom, the Sultan commanded: 'Let each of you recount the most remarkable case of justice you have ever administered, that I may see who among you truly understands the human heart.'

The Chief of Cairo spoke first: 'Sire, I once captured a man who broke into a bakery at midnight. When I examined him, I found he had stolen neither gold nor silver, but only three loaves of bread. His wife had given birth that night, and his three young children were starving. Instead of cutting off his hand, I paid the baker for the bread, secured the man employment in the public granaries, and saw him become an honest citizen. Justice must not punish hunger where industry can provide work.'

The Chief of Fustat spoke next: 'A merchant accused his neighbor of stealing a bag of pearls. The neighbor denied the theft, swearing by the sacred oaths. Observing the accuser’s servants, I noticed a young boy who turned pale whenever the pearls were mentioned. Taking the boy aside with gentle kindness, he confessed that he had hidden the pearls in the garden wall to buy toys. I restored the pearls to the merchant, saved the innocent neighbor from execution, and counseled the boy’s father. True justice protects the innocent by seeing through appearances.'

The Chief of Qus spoke third: 'Two brothers quarreled bitterly over their father’s inheritance of an orchard, ready to slay each other. I ordered the orchard divided equally, but commanded that neither brother could harvest his fruit until he had delivered one basket of his finest figs to his brother's door. Within a month, the daily exchange of gifts dissolved their anger, and they embraced as friends. Justice must heal severed families rather than merely divide property.'

The Sultan smiled with profound satisfaction, declaring: 'Blessed is the kingdom whose guardians rule with mercy, truth, and reconciliation rather than the naked blade.'
moral: Fair justice requires discernment, mercy, and understanding the root cause behind every human action.
